questions.question: Explain the purpose of the .pl file extension in Perl programming
questions.solution_html:
• ● Serves as the standard file extension to designate a plain text file containing executable Perl
  • code.
  • ● Helps the operating system and development environments recognize and properly
  • associate the script with the Perl interpreter.
  • ● Differentiates execution scripts from reusable script libraries or modules which typically use
  • the .pm extension.
  • ● Enhances code organization and portability across different command-line environments.
questions.final_answer: ● Enhances code organization and portability across different command-line environments

questions.question: Describe the working of the for loop and foreach loop in Perl.
questions.solution_html:
• ● for loop: Typically used for traditional, index-based numeric counters with explicit
  • initialization, condition, and re-evaluation expressions.
  • ● foreach loop: Designed to iterate seamlessly through every individual element of an array or
  • a list from beginning to end.
  • ● Aliasing: In a foreach loop, the loop control variable acts as a direct alias to the current
  • element; modifying it alters the original array element.
  • ● Interchangability: In Perl, the keywords for and foreach are technically interchangeable, but
  • stylistic conventions prefer choosing them based on readability.
questions.final_answer: stylistic conventions prefer choosing them based on readability

questions.solution_html:

questions.question: Use Bio::AlignIO to read an alignment and obtain the sequence information / from the alignment.
questions.solution_html:
• Use Bio::AlignIO to read an alignment and obtain the sequence information from the
  • alignment.
  • ● Initialize a Bio::AlignIO streaming input object by defining the target filename and format
  • parameter.
  • ● Use the next_aln() method to pull alignment records systematically from the initialized file
  • stream.
  • ● Iterate over individual sequence objects contained within the alignment layer via the
  • each_seq() method to read information.
  • use Bio::AlignIO;
  • $in = Bio::AlignIO->new(-file => "align.fasta", -format => "fasta");
  • while (my $aln = $in->next_aln()) {
  • foreach my $seq ($aln->each_seq()) {
  • print "ID: ", $seq->id(), " Sequence: ", $seq->seq(), "\n";
  • }

questions.question: Explain operator precedence and associativity in Perl with suitable examples. / Explain the procedure for executing a Perl script from the command line with
questions.solution_html:
• ● Operator Precedence: Determines the parsing priority and execution order when distinct
  • operators are placed together in a single statement. ((3 Marks))
  • ● Associativity: Specifies the direction of evaluation (left-to-right or right-to-left) when multiple
  • operators sharing identical precedence appear together. ((3 Marks))
  • ● Precedence Example: In 5 + 2 * 3, multiplication (*) holds a higher precedence ranking than
  • addition (+), computing to 11 instead of 21.
  • ● Associativity Example: The assignment operator (=) evaluates right-to-left, allowing chain
  • operations like $a = $b = 10.
questions.final_answer: operations like $a = $b = 10

questions.question: Identify the different types of anchors used in Perl pattern matching and state the / purpose of each.
questions.solution_html:
• each.
  • ● Definition of Anchors: Special regular expression metacharacters that do not match
  • individual text characters, but instead lock matches to explicit positions within strings. (2
  • Marks)
  • ● Caret Anchor (^): Forces a successful pattern match exclusively at the absolute starting
  • boundary position of the evaluation string. ((2 Marks))
  • ● Dollar Anchor ($): Compels a pattern match to align precisely with the absolute final
  • boundary position or right before a trailing newline of a string. ((2 Marks))
  • ● Word Boundaries (\b and \B): \b asserts a boundary position between an alphanumeric word
  • character and a non-word character space; \B negates this check. ((2 Marks))
  • ● Example 1: if ($str =~ /^ATG/) checks if a sequence string explicitly initiates with a start
  • codon.
  • ● Example 2: if ($str =~ /TAA$/) checks if a sequence string explicitly terminates with a stop
  • codon.
questions.final_answer: Option (b) : \b asserts a boundary position between an alphanumeric word
